title: A pricing page for an independent hotel
metaTitle: What an independent hotel pricing page shows
excerpt: A pricing page should show what the rate includes, what it does not, and how to check dates. Travelers use it to judge fit before they do the arithmetic.
alt: A white wall covered with framed prints, small plants, and two floating shelves, each piece kept separate the way a rate's inclusions should be.
caption: Each frame on the wall is separate and readable. A rate should be that easy to compare. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on a hotel pricing page?
faqs.answer: The shape of the rate, what is included, what is not, and a way to check dates. Name midweek, weekend, and seasonal differences if they exist. A single from-price with no conditions teaches the wrong number.

faqs.question: Should a small hotel hide the rate until checkout?
faqs.answer: No. A traveler comparing three stays will ask the shape of the price anyway. Put breakfast, tax, parking, and extra-guest fees where the eye lands. Silence reads as included, and the invoice then feels like a trick.

faqs.question: Do I need a price calculator?
faqs.answer: The date checker is the calculator that matters. A tool that demands an email before it shows a number is a mailing list. State the pattern in a short table so a guest can judge fit in about a minute.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
An independent hotel pricing page is where a traveler comparing three stays decides whether the rate fits the room, before they do the arithmetic. Show what is included, what is not, and how to check dates. If they will ask the shape of the price anyway, put that shape on the page.

People do not read a tariff as literature. Nielsen Norman Group found that visitors read only about a quarter of the text on pages they actually open. A pricing page that buries the Saturday rate inside a paragraph will be judged on the one number that happens to be visible, or it will be abandoned for a site that states the number plainly.

## Fit before the total

The traveler is not ready to multiply nights. They are asking a rougher question: is this the kind of stay I thought it was? A calm room at a calm price is a fit. A calm room with a resort fee, a parking surprise, and a breakfast that costs as much as the room is a different product. The page exists to make that difference visible.

Lead with the room the homepage already showed, then the rate that belongs to it. Name the conditions in the same breath: midweek, a weekend night, a longer minimum, a high season. A single "from" with no conditions is a number that will be resented later. The resentment is fair. The page taught them the wrong price.

Judging fit is allowed to be quick. A short table beats a story. Room, what you sleep in, what the rate covers, what sits outside it. A traveler can compare that table with the other two tabs. They cannot compare three essays about the meaning of hospitality.

Google's people-first guidance asks whether someone can leave having learned enough to reach their goal. On this page the goal is a yes or a no about fit. A page that withholds the shape of the rate fails that test, even when the prose is warm.

## What "included" has to name

"Includes" is a claim. Make it a list a person can check at the desk. Breakfast, if it is truly in the rate, with the hours. Tax treatment, in plain words: whether the figure on the page is the figure they pay. Wi-Fi, if you feel you must say it. Parking, with the number of spaces and whether a car is realistic on your street. A late checkout rule, if it is real and not a favor the owner sometimes grants.

Write each inclusion as a thing the guest receives, not as a brand value. "A set breakfast in the small room off the courtyard, until 10" is an inclusion. "Thoughtful touches" is not. The traveler is trying to see whether the rate replaces three separate purchases or only the bed.

If breakfast is the reason people return, give it two sentences and stop. What is on the table, where they sit, and whether a dietary need can be met if they say so the day before. Do not attach a manifesto about ingredients. The other pages can carry the cook. This page carries the bill.

Match the words to the checker. If the booking step says "room only" and this page says "stay includes breakfast," you have two products. Pick one and use it in both places. A mismatch here is how a good property starts to feel slippery.

## What is not included

The exclusions are part of the fit. Name them without apology and without a joke. An extra guest. A pet fee and the rules that come with it. A cot. Parking when the rate does not cover it. Minibar or honesty bar, if the prices are not obvious in the room. A cleaning charge that appears only on a one-night stay.

Put exclusions where the eye lands, not in a footer policy in eight-point type. A traveler comparing three stays will assume silence means "included." When the invoice says otherwise, the photograph of the room will not save the stay.

If a charge depends on the season, say the season. If it depends on the room, say the room. "Fees may apply" is a sentence that creates work for the desk and doubt for the guest. Replace it with the fee, or remove the fee.

City or occupancy taxes vary by place. You do not need a legal essay. You need one true line: included in the figure, or added at payment, and roughly what kind of amount. If you cannot state it, the page is not ready to publish. The desk already knows the answer. Write that answer down.

## The shape of the price

The shape is the pattern, not a fake calculator. Many independent hotels have a midweek rate, a Friday or Saturday rate, and a stretch of the year when both move. Say so. Show the pattern beside the room it belongs to. If August is different from March, the page should say August is different from March.

A calculator that asks for an email before it shows a number is a lead form wearing a pricing costume. Skip it. The date checker is the calculator that matters, and it should not collect a newsletter subscription on the way.

Do not hide a two-night minimum inside the checker alone. If Saturdays require two nights, the pricing page says that next to the Saturday rate. The traveler can then decide whether the shape fits the trip they actually have. A one-night visitor who learns the rule after six fields of a form will not feel looked after. They will feel caught.

Rooms that share a building and not a rate need their own lines. The small double and the courtyard room are different products. Averaging them into one "rooms from" number teaches the wrong lesson, then the checker corrects it too late. List them. Three lines are not a spreadsheet. Three lines are respect for the comparison the traveler is already doing.

If a rate includes a dinner on certain nights, say which nights. If a longer stay changes the nightly figure, say the threshold: from the fourth night, or for a week. The shape should be learnable in a minute. Nielsen's finding about how little text gets read is the constraint. Design the page so the minute is enough.

## How to check dates from here

Every rate block needs the same next step. Check these dates. The button should carry the room type when you have more than one, so the traveler does not arrive in a general search and lose the courtyard room they just decided they wanted.

Say what the checker will confirm: availability for those nights, and the total for that pattern, including the items you listed. If the checker cannot show tax, repeat the one-line tax note beside the button. Do not promise a total the system will not show.

A traveler who is ready to book should not be sent back to the homepage to hunt for the widget. The pricing page is often the second visit, or the visit from a comparison email they sent themselves. Treat it as a place where the decision can finish.

If the dates are flexible, offer the pattern in words so they can choose a cheaper night on purpose. "Sunday to Thursday is the lower rate" helps a person whose dates can move. It also keeps you from pretending every night costs the same, which your regulars already know is untrue.

## What to stop writing

Stop explaining that small hotels have costs. The guest knows. The page is not a defense of the rate. It is a description of it. A paragraph about the price of linen does not help a comparison. A line about what the rate covers does.

Stop the adjective stack. Charming, curated, intimate, elevated. None of those words changes the Saturday number. If the room is small, the pricing page can say small, because small is part of fit. People who want small will stay. People who do not will leave cleanly, which is kinder than a surprise at the door.

Stop a seasonal essay that never states the season's rate. "Summer is our favorite time in the garden" is a feeling. The August rate is the fact. You may keep one sentence of season if the rate sits next to it. You may not keep the sentence instead of the rate.

Read the page as if you were paying. Circle every number and every "includes." If a circle has no neighbor that explains it, write the neighbor. If a paragraph has no circle, ask whether the paragraph is doing a job. Most of them are not.

## After the rate makes sense

A traveler who understands the rate next wants each part of the stay named in their own words: breakfast, the desk, the room, the street. That is a services page, not a second tariff. [What each part of the stay actually includes](/blog/the-services-page-an-independent-hotel-actually-needs) is the next piece, because a price without those boundaries still leaves the comparison half done.

When you want that page built as a clear offer rather than a brochure, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the rate sheet you already send by email. The page should be at least as honest as that sheet.
